newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finnish SDP group leader says EMU too big risk now.
newsitem.headline: Finnish SDP group leader says EMU too big risk now.

text.p: Erkki Tuomioja, newly elected chairman of the Finnish Social Democratic Party's (SDP) parliamentary group, was quoted on Tuesday as saying EMU was too big a risk and should be put on ice for at least 10 years.

"Creating monetary union without a sufficiently strong deepening of economic cooperation is a very big risk for all of Europe. It is a risk so big that it should not be taken," Tuomioja was quoted as saying in an interview in regional daily Etela-Suomen Sanomat.
His views are opposed to those of Prime Minister and SDP party chairman Paavo Lipponen, a staunch EMU supporter.

The SDP is the biggest party in government and parliament. Tuomioja, known already as an outspoken EMU critic, is becoming SDP group chairman after Pertti Paasio, who was elected on October 20 to represent Finland in the European Parliament.
According to Finnish political practice, cabinet ministers are guided by their respective parliamentary group.
Tuomioja said the third phase of EMU was not ready for implementation as early as its scheduled 1999 kick-off.
"I think the plan is immature (but) it could be a quite viable target for the (EU) after some 10 years," he said.
EMU was being forced on Europe against the wish of most citizens, he said.

"The efforts to speed up the deepening of a political and economic union without any certainty about whether it will come about -- and which today most Europeans oppose -- are incomprehensible," Tuomioja said.

"Even when everyone knows that in most countries a majority, and in any case in all countries a significant share of the people, take a doubtful or negative attitude to monetarey union, nobody at (decision-making) tables voice their doubts," he said.
He said he had spoken recently with German SDP politicians, many of whom acknowledged the weaknesses of EMU.
Tuomioja said it did not bode well that some countries, like France, openly relied on budget tricks to meet the Maastricht deficit criterion.
But he said he supported the Lipponen government's drive to put the Finnish economy in shape so the parliament would have a real choice on joining the third phase of EMU from the start.
Tuomioja also said he supported Lipponen as prime minister, although he wished that social democratic goals were more clearly visible in the coalition's policies.
Dissent by individual SDP MPs on isolated issues was no threat to the unity of the party nor to cooperation within the government, he said.
